title: Linear Regression
body:
Everything before this block described one variable at a time. Regression is about **two**: an
independent variable $x$ you have, a dependent $y$ you want, and a line connecting them.

$$
\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

Start with a **scatter diagram**, because it answers the questions no summary statistic can: is the
relationship linear at all, is the spread constant, are there outliers pulling the fit. Fitting a
line to data you have not plotted is how you end up describing a parabola with a slope of zero.

## Least squares

The line is chosen to minimise the sum of squared **residuals**, $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$, the
vertical gaps between the points and the line:

$$
\text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2
$$

Set both partial derivatives to zero and the answer drops out in closed form:

$$
\beta_1 = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2}
= r\,\frac{s_y}{s_x},
\qquad
\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1\bar{x}
$$

Two things fall straight out of those. **The line always passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$**, by
the second equation. And the slope is [[Correlation|Pearson's $r$]] rescaled by the two standard
deviations, so regression and correlation are computed from the same three sums; $r$ says how
strong, $\beta_1$ says how steep, and they are not the same question.

Squared residuals rather than absolute ones for the reasons [[Variance]] gives: differentiable,
additive, closed form. The cost is the same too, which is that a single outlier dominates the fit
because its residual gets squared.

## The same object as [[Least Squares]]

**This is the best pairing in the MATH block and both notes are written to say so.**
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) reaches these exact coefficients without doing any
calculus. Stack the data into a matrix $X$ with a column of ones and a column of $x_i$, and fitting
is solving $X\boldsymbol{\beta} \approx \mathbf{y}$, which has no exact solution because there are
more rows than unknowns. The closest reachable vector is the [[Projection]] of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the
column space, so the residual must be orthogonal to every column, giving the **normal equations**

$$
X^TX\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = X^T\mathbf{y}
$$

Those are the same two equations obtained above by differentiating. $\text{SSR} = \|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2$,
so minimising a sum of squares and dropping a perpendicular onto a subspace are one operation in two
languages. Statistics differentiates, linear algebra projects, and the answer is identical.

Two facts the geometry makes obvious that the calculus hides: **the residuals sum to zero and are
uncorrelated with $x$ by construction**, because orthogonality says so. Which is why a residual plot
is diagnostic.

## Residual plots

Plot $e_i$ against $x_i$ or against $\hat{y}_i$. Under a correct model it is a formless band around
zero, and any structure at all is the model being wrong rather than merely imprecise:

| Pattern | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| curve | relationship is not linear; transform $x$ or add a term |
| funnel widening | non-constant variance, so the standard errors are wrong |
| one point far out | outlier, and check its leverage before deleting anything |
| pattern against time | the observations are not independent |

The four assumptions behind the inference (not behind the fit itself) are linearity, independence,
constant variance, and roughly [[Normal Distribution|normal]] residuals. The fit needs none of them;
the [[Confidence Interval|intervals]] and tests on $\beta_1$ need all four.

## Inference and prediction

$\beta_1$ is an estimate from a sample, so it has a standard error and everything from block 4
applies: a $t$-test of $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ ("no linear relationship") and a confidence interval for
the slope. See [[Hypothesis Testing]].

**Do not extrapolate.** The line is evidence about the range of $x$ you observed and nothing
outside it, and the classic failures (predicting record times to reach zero, fitting an early
epidemic curve forwards) are all this rule being broken.

## Where it goes: this is the simplest machine learning model

Least squares regression **is** supervised learning with one feature. Same objects, different
vocabulary:

| Statistics | [[MACHINE LEARNING]] |
|---|---|
| independent variable $x$ | feature |
| dependent variable $y$ | label or target |
| coefficients $\beta$ | weights, see [[Weights]] |
| intercept $\beta_0$ | bias term, see [[Bias Term]] |
| SSR | squared-error [[Loss Function]] |
| solving the normal equations | training |

The one real difference is **how the minimum is found**. This course solves it in closed form, which
works because squared error over a linear model is a convex quadratic with an exact solution.
[[Gradient Descent]] walks downhill to the same point instead, which is slower and pointless here,
and is the only option once the model is non-linear and the closed form stops existing. **Two routes
to one line**, and that is worth stating plainly because it is where this course hands over to
[[Neural Network|neural networks]]: a network is this with the linearity dropped and gradient
descent kept.

Adding more predictors gives **multiple regression**, $\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \cdots +
\beta_kx_k$, which is the matrix form above with more columns and needs no new theory. And the model
only has to be linear **in the coefficients**, so columns of $x^2$ or $\log x$ fit curves with the
same machinery; see [[Least Squares]].

When the response is a category rather than a number, squared error is the wrong loss and the line
is the wrong shape. That is [[Logistic Regression]] and [[Binary Classification]], which swap in
[[Log Loss]] and lose the closed form.

## Related

- [[Correlation]]: the strength of the relationship, and $r^2$
- [[Least Squares]] and [[Projection]] (MATH 2303): the geometric derivation of these equations
- [[ANOVA]]: the same sums-of-squares decomposition
- [[Descriptive Statistics]]: a scatter diagram is the two-variable member of that family
- [[SGD Classification]] and [[Gradient Descent]]: the iterative route to the same minimum
